batchName: Late Republic: Spartacus and Pompey (78-63 BCE) - Easy Batch 2
chapterName: Late Republic: Spartacus and Pompey (78-63 BCE)

questions.question: Which mountain did the escaped gladiators retreat to after plundering the countryside?
questions.explanation: The runaways took refuge on Mount Vesuvius, the volcano above the Bay of Naples. A praetor tried to starve them out by blocking the only path down.
questions.sourceQuote: The runaways beat a small force from Capua, plundered the countryside and retreated to Mount Vesuvius, the volcano above the Bay of Naples.

questions.question: Why did Lucullus' soldiers mutiny and refuse to march against Mithridates?
options: They grumbled only their general got rich
They had not been paid for years
Their homes in Italy had been raided
questions.explanation: The weary troops resented that only Lucullus was growing rich. Their mutiny let Mithridates recover his kingdom, and Rome decided to replace Lucullus.
questions.sourceQuote: But his weary soldiers grumbled that only their general was getting rich.

questions.question: Mithridates, Rome's most stubborn enemy in the East, was king of which realm?
questions.explanation: Mithridates ruled Pontus, on the southern shore of the Black Sea. In 88 BC he had ordered the massacre of Roman and Italian settlers across Asia Minor.
questions.sourceQuote: Mithridates, king of Pontus, a realm on the southern shore of the Black Sea, was Rome's most stubborn enemy in the East.

questions.question: Which city did Pompey capture in 63 BC after a three-month siege?
questions.explanation: Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, a year after turning Syria into a Roman province.
questions.sourceQuote: Meanwhile Pompey turned Syria into a Roman province in 64 BC and in 63 BC captured Jerusalem after a three-month siege.

questions.question: How long did Pompey's entire war against the pirates take?
questions.explanation: The whole campaign lasted just three months, ending with the storming of the pirates' last Cilician strongholds.
questions.sourceQuote: The whole war took just three months.

questions.question: Which law of 67 BC gave Pompey his sweeping command against the Mediterranean pirates?
questions.explanation: A tribune of the plebs proposed the Gabinian Law at Pompey's urging. The Senate feared giving one man such power, but the people voted it through.
questions.sourceQuote: In 67 BC a tribune of the plebs (*tribunus plebis*), an official elected to defend ordinary citizens, proposed the Gabinian Law (*lex Gabinia*) at Pompey's urging.

questions.question: In which city was the gladiator school from which Spartacus and his companions broke out in 73 BC?
questions.explanation: The escape began at a gladiator school in Capua, a wealthy city south of Rome. Around 70 men fought their way out armed with kitchen choppers and roasting spits.
questions.sourceQuote: In 73 BC, about 200 gladiators at a school in Capua, a wealthy city south of Rome, plotted to escape.

questions.question: According to the ancient historians, how did Spartacus meet his end?
options: He fell fighting, body never found
He escaped by ship to Thrace
He was murdered by his own men
questions.explanation: Every ancient historian says Spartacus died fighting in the final battle by the Silarius River, yet his body was never found.
questions.sourceQuote: Every ancient historian says Spartacus fell fighting, though his body was never found.

questions.question: What was a slave's legal status under the law of the Roman Republic?
options: A dependent client of the family
A free man bound by debt
questions.explanation: Roman law treated a slave as property. An owner could beat, maim or even kill his own slaves without any legal consequence.
questions.sourceQuote: Under the law of the Republic, a slave was property, not a person.

questions.question: Pompey's soldiers hailed him as 'the Great' (Magnus), in imitation of which famous conqueror?
questions.explanation: His troops named him Magnus after Alexander the Great, and Pompey made the name officially his. He also forced the dictator to grant him a triumph at an unheard-of young age.
questions.sourceQuote: His own soldiers, however, hailed him as "the Great" (*Magnus*), after Alexander the Great, and he made the name officially his.
